newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan, U.S. fail to reach agreement at WTO talks.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan, U.S. fail to reach agreement at WTO talks.

text.p: Taipei and Washington ended their latest round of negotiations over Taiwan's bid to join the World Trade Organisation with no significant agreements, Taiwan officials said on Thursday.
But officials said Taiwan has agreed in principle to open more government purchases to foreign sellers if the island is allowed to join the world trade body.

"Our government will agree to sign WTO's Government Procurement Agreement, but we have not decided how much to open our market," a Taiwan Board of Foreign Trade spokeswoman quoted the board's deputy director general Chen Jui-lung as saying.
Taipei made the pledge after it concluded on Wednesday six days of talks with the United States on the island's WTO bid.
"It was a step towards the right direction, and we believe we are making progress toward narrowing our differences," Chen was quoted as saying.
The American Institute in Taiwan, the unofficial U.S. office in Taipei in the absence of diplomatic ties, declined to comment.
In particular, the two sides have yet to agree on how much Taiwan should liberalise its agricultural, tobacco and alcohol industries, Taiwan officials said.
Taipei currently runs a monopoly on the island's tobacco and alcohol markets, and it subsidises most farm products by setting government-guaranteed prices.
The government has said it would gradually loosen its hold on tobacco and liquor. It said on Monday it would streamline the agricultural subsidy system to conform with WTO practises.
The two sides also disagree on the extent Taiwan would carry out the government purchase agreement, the Taipei side said.

"Just think of this like any transaction. The seller wants to sell at the highest price, and the buyer wants to cut the price as far as possible. That is the difference we are trying to work out," another Taiwan official said.

She said American representatives claimed the U.S. has provided up to US$77.7 billion for foreign buyers under its adoption of the government purchase agreement, while Taiwan's scheme would provide only $15.4 billion.

Taiwan, which hopes to become a WTO member in 1997, has so far held talks with WTO members South Africa, Turkey, Malaysia, the Czech Republic, Solvakia, Hungary, the Philippines, El Salvador, Colombia, Uruguay, Australia and the United States.
Taiwan applied in 1990 to join WTO's predecessor, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, under the name of Chinese Taipei. GATT was replaced by WTO in January 1995.
Taiwan has made major concessions in the past few years in a bid to join the world body, allowing more imports and opening up its domestic markets and even government-controlled industries.

China, which regards Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war separated them in 1949, says Taipei is not entitled to membership of international organisations. China's bid to join GATT by the end of 1994 was rejected.
